St. Seraphim of Vyritsa

Saints

St. Seraphim of Vyritsa

St. Vasily Nikolaevich Muravyev · St. Basil Muraviev · St. Varnava Muravyev

Period
1865/1866–1949;birth year differs in published accounts
Region
Yaroslavl province;Saint Petersburg;Vyritsa
Titles / vocation
Monastic · Priest · Elder
Commemoration
March21 / April3 New Style in the OCA’s account

Introduction

St. Seraphim was a married merchant before becoming a monk and elder. The OCA, Minsk life and Saint Petersburg reference work agree on his later ministry at Vyritsa but differ on parts of the chronology.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

Reposed after long illness in1949

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The Minsk life describes Vasily’s father’s death and his childhood employment in Saint Petersburg. He rises from shop errands to management and a fur business. His marriage to Olga includes the birth of son Nikolai and the death of their infant daughter. The couple supports churches, almshouses and patients who need care. Their eventual monastic vocation is presented as a mutual decision after decades of family and charitable life. The account prints April 13, 1866 New Calendar for his birth, while the OCA gives 1865.

[2] Published life,April3,2026;identified modern biographical sources · Muravyov family,trade,charity and printed birth date

Life and notable events

Antonov’s reference entry records vows in 1920 as Varnava, priesthood in 1921, and the schema name Seraphim with his role as Lavra confessor in 1927. It dates the move to Vyritsa to summer 1930. These dated statements are separately attributed because the OCA says it does not know his first tonsure details and places settlement at Vyritsa in 1933 after imprisonment. The entries cannot simply be combined into one apparently uncontested chronology.

[3] English web entry;identified bibliography · Lavra offices and1930 settlement

The OCA’s received life attributes clairvoyance and healing to him and describes visitors seeking consolation during illness and persecution. It also recounts searches of his cell and an attempted arrest stopped after a doctor warned of his condition. These are that source’s narrative claims.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Vyritsa ministry and illness

The Minsk account records Nikolai’s arrest and execution in 1941 and identifies the elder’s wife, then schema-nun Seraphima, as his attendant until her 1945 death. It describes his prayer on a stone during the war as a reported feature of his life.

[2] Published life,April3,2026;identified modern biographical sources · Family losses and war

Death and martyrdom

The OCA gives March 21, 1949 and explicitly supplies April 3 New Style. It describes weakness, remaining in bed and receiving visitors before repose. His death is not an execution; the title elder does not itself establish martyrdom.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Final illness and repose

The Minsk account describes final Communion and repose around two in the morning on April 3, 1949.

[2] Published life,April3,2026;identified modern biographical sources · Closing account

Writings and legacy

The OCA records burial beside the Kazan church at Vyritsa and glorification by the Russian Church in August 2000. It describes the village becoming a place of pilgrimage.

[1] Official Orthodox commemoration and received life · Burial and glorification

The reference work locates his relics in the chapel near the Kazan church’s altar and notes his reputation for spiritual healing. Its bibliography identifies Filimonov’s 1999 life and a 2003 study of the Muravyov family, providing leads for further historical research.

[3] English web entry;identified bibliography · Closing entry and bibliography

The Minsk life records a wooden chapel built over the grave in 2000, with Seraphima buried nearby.

[2] Published life,April3,2026;identified modern biographical sources · Closing commemoration

Antonov locates his 1931–1945 home at7 Pilnoy Avenue and records the wartime stone-prayer tradition. These particulars belong to the reference work’s regional history of Vyritsa.

[3] English web entry;identified bibliography · Residence and wartime remembrance
